title: David Found Strength in the Lord
lead: In a moment of total collapse, strength can still be found in God.
questions: Who around you has stayed behind with the supplies out of sheer exhaustion, and does your way of dividing the plunder include them?
What do you do when no one comes to strengthen you, and what would it look like for you to find strength in the Lord among the ashes?
What is your next right step in the matter you keep only grieving over?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: David at Ziklag is not an innocent man struck by misfortune. He was looking for refuge from Saul, so he settled among the Philistines, and for sixteen months he built his life on a lie, deceiving King Achish, who trusted him. The Bible reports it without excuses. And then, in the space of one morning, it all went up in flames: the Amalekites raided Ziklag, burned the city and carried off the women and children. Six hundred hardened warriors “wept until they had no strength left to weep.” The embittered men quickly found someone to blame: they talked of stoning David. Many of us know this kind of rock bottom: a despair that is especially heavy because the disaster came partly through our own fault.

And then comes the most important sentence of the story: “But David found strength in the LORD his God.” The Hebrew verb here is reflexive: David strengthened himself in the LORD. A person’s action and God’s gift are held together in one word. No one came to help him. Once, in his darkest days, Jonathan had strengthened him in God; now he had to do it himself. That strength had an immediate, practical sequel: “Bring me the ephod.” David asked God for guidance, and the Lord answered a man who had been deceiving others for months without a word of reproach: “Pursue them… for you will surely overtake them and rescue the captives.” God doesn’t wait for a person to shape up before He will be with him.

The key to the pursuit was lying in a field: an abandoned, sick Egyptian slave, left behind by his Amalekite master like broken equipment. David’s men fed him first and only then asked who he was. He led them to the raiders’ camp. Every last captive was recovered. And when the victors wanted to shut the two hundred exhausted men who had stayed with the supplies at the Brook Besor out of the plunder, David laid down a rule that has held in Israel ever since: “The share of the one who went to battle will match the share of the one who stayed with the supplies.” The victory was the Lord’s gift, so no one could turn it into a ranking of merit. A church in which the weary are a lower class stops understanding where its wealth comes from.

The section “There Is Hope When Life Falls Apart” is about loss, about tears, about collapse and about our own guilt. Today’s story brings all of these threads together. David at Ziklag was not an innocent man struck by misfortune. For sixteen months this man had built his life on a lie, and now he stood in the ashes. And yet from this very story comes one of the most important pieces of biblical advice about what to do when you have nothing left.

sections.heading: An Escape That Looked Sensible
paragraphs: Before the events at Ziklag, David made a decision the Bible doesn’t praise. He concluded that sooner or later he would die at Saul’s hand, so he fled where the king couldn’t reach him: to the Philistines. King Achish of Gath took him in and gave him the little town of Ziklag. For sixteen months David lived there off raids on the surrounding tribes, and he lied to the Philistine ruler about whom he was raiding. The text reports all of this without a single word of excuse and without any comment. It doesn’t soften it, doesn’t explain it, doesn’t make a saint out of David. The anointed future king of Israel is lying to a pagan who trusted him, and the reader is meant to see it. The Bible is honest about its heroes in a way we rarely manage about ours.

sections.heading: An Angel of God on a Foreign Payroll
paragraphs: The most bitter scene in this story takes place before the disaster. The Philistines are mustering their armies against Israel, and David is marching with them, in Achish’s rear guard. The Philistine commanders object: what are these Hebrews doing here? And David is sent back. Then Achish says words to him that send a shiver down the spine: “As surely as the LORD lives, you have been upright in my sight.” A pagan swears by the name of David’s God and adds: “I know that you are as pleasing in my sight as an angel of God.” A man who has been lied to again and again praises the deceiver for his honesty. In this scene the Philistine king comes off better than the Lord’s anointed, and the narrator whitewashes nothing. But there is another side: the suspicion of the hostile generals rescues David from a situation with no good way out, a march against his own people. God can rescue a person by the hands of people who don’t trust Him. Sometimes being sent away empty-handed is grace in disguise.

sections.heading: The Third Day: Smoke
paragraphs: David gets back to Ziklag after three days of forced marching. What he finds there is ashes: the Amalekites had raided the Negev, “attacked Ziklag, and burned it down,” and carried off the women and children. The text notes a detail that was obvious back then: they hadn’t killed anyone, because captives were merchandise. But the husbands and fathers standing in the ashes of their homes knew only that their families were gone. “So David and the troops with him lifted up their voices and wept until they had no strength left to weep.” Professional soldiers, men who had been through a lot, weep until their tears run out. The Bible doesn’t tell men to keep a stiff upper lip. It records the weeping of six hundred tough men without a hint of embarrassment.

sections.heading: They Spoke of Stoning Him
paragraphs: The embittered warriors start looking for someone to blame, and they find him quickly: “And David was greatly distressed because the people spoke of stoning him, because the soul of every man grieved for his sons and daughters.” The same men who had followed him into exile are now picking up stones. And it’s hard to be surprised: it was his decisions that had brought them to Ziklag, his politics that had left the town undefended. Let’s count what David lost in a single morning: his home, both his wives, everything he owned, the trust of his men, and all of it at the end of a road he himself had chosen. In a situation like that, despair is especially heavy, because you know part of the blame is yours. Many of us know this kind of rock bottom. And right here comes the most important sentence of the story.

sections.heading: He Found Strength in the LORD
paragraphs: “But David found strength in the LORD his God.” The Hebrew form of this verb is reflexive, and older translations render it literally: “David strengthened himself in Yahweh his God” (WEB). Both sides of the sentence are true at once: it was David’s action, and it was God’s gift, in a single word. The future king has nothing left on the outside, so he reaches to where the Amalekite fire never reached. The text also says something by what it doesn’t say: no one came to David. A few years earlier, in the worst days of his flight, Jonathan had come to him and, as it is written, “strengthened his hand in God.” Now Jonathan is far away, with his father, in a war from which he will not return. So David does for himself what a friend once did for him. There are moments in life when no one will call. A person who knows how to find strength in God then will come through them differently from someone who can draw strength only from other people. In the background of this story stands the book’s other man, backed against the wall in those same days: Saul. He too is at rock bottom, but over the years he himself had cut off every channel of help: he slaughtered the Lord’s priests, he lost Samuel, and the ephod went off with the surviving priest to David’s camp. What he had left was the medium at Endor and the night before defeat. Two broken men, one book, two directions. Despair doesn’t choose for us. We choose which way we will turn.

sections.heading: Bring Me the Ephod
paragraphs: With David, finding strength has an immediate, practical sequel: “Bring me the ephod.” Abiathar the priest, the only survivor of the massacre at Nob, brings the garment used for seeking God’s counsel, and David asks whether he should pursue the raiders. And God answers a man with sixteen months of lies behind him without a single word of reproach: “Pursue them… for you will surely overtake them and rescue the captives.” That answer holds the whole theology of this chapter. God doesn’t wait for a person to shape up before He will be with him and work through him. He doesn’t settle accounts before giving help. The accounting will come in its time; David’s life will remind him of that more than once. But on the day a person at rock bottom asks God for the way, the Lord answers.

sections.heading: The Egyptian in the Field
paragraphs: During the pursuit something happens that is easy to overlook, and yet it is the key to the whole operation. David’s men find a half-dead man in a field. Before anyone asks him anything, they give him bread, water, a piece of a fig cake and raisins, because he hasn’t eaten for three days. Only then comes the question of who he is. “I am an Egyptian… the slave of an Amalekite. My master abandoned me three days ago when I fell ill.” The Amalekite left a sick man in a field like a piece of broken equipment. This abandoned slave will lead David to the raiders’ camp. The whole rescue of six hundred families passed through a man someone had judged useless, and through people who fed him first and only afterward checked whether he would be worth it. Who knows how many of God’s solutions are waiting for us in people we walk past because they don’t look useful.

sections.heading: The Law of the Weary
paragraphs: At the Brook Besor, two hundred of David’s six hundred men have no strength to go on. They stay with the supplies. Four hundred catch up with the Amalekites and recover every last captive: “Nothing was missing, young or old, son or daughter.” On the way back, though, a dispute breaks out, and the Bible describes it sharply: “all the wicked and worthless men” among the victors demand that the men from the brook get only their wives and children back, with no share of the plunder. They didn’t fight, so they didn’t earn it. David’s answer became law in Israel: “My brothers, you must not do this with what the LORD has given us… The share of the one who went to battle will match the share of the one who stayed with the supplies. They will share alike.” The man who that morning was one step away from being stoned is defending the weakest in his unit that afternoon. The victory was the Lord’s gift, David said, so no one can turn it into a ranking of merit. A church in which the weary are a lower class stops understanding where its wealth comes from. Every congregation knows this: it has people on the front line and people with the supplies, the ones in the kitchen, the ones who clean, the ones who quietly care for others, and the ones who this year simply couldn’t go any farther. The law of Besor is clear: an equal share. Not out of pity, but because the plunder is God’s grace anyway.

The story has a short epilogue that shows David had learned for the future. He sends part of the plunder to the elders of Judah in more than a dozen towns where he had spent time during his years on the run, with a short note: “Here is a gift for you from the plunder of the LORD’s enemies.” The man who had nothing that morning is sharing by evening. Among the towns that receive gifts is Hebron, the very place where Judah would later anoint David king. Generosity shown on the day he got his family back built bridges for his whole future. Grace that is shared comes back to us from the direction we least expect.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: If your life has just fallen apart, and partly through your own fault, this story is for you. First: your own guilt does not close the road to God. The Lord answered David on a day when he had no moral right to expect anything. Second: there are times when no one will come to strengthen you, and then you may do what David did: turn to the Lord yourself, with no go-between, without a good mood, among the ashes. Third: you recognize real strength by what a person does next. David didn’t receive a feeling of relief from God; he received a way forward: a question, a pursuit, a concrete next step. Sometimes the only form of hope available on a given day is doing the next right thing. And one more important thing for us as a church: once he had recovered everything, David didn’t forget the weary men with the supplies. The hope that comes back to us usually arrives through the hands of those who have experienced it themselves.
